# In Defence of Idlers

Boswell once complained to Dr. Johnson that we grow weary when we are idle. Johnson would not let the remark pass. We grow weary, he said, only because others are busy and we want for company. If we were all idle together, nobody would grow weary at all; we should simply entertain one another. I have always loved that answer. It turns a supposed weakness of the idle man into a fault of his surroundings, and it suggests a world I should very much like to live in.

It is not the world we have. At present everyone is pressed, from the cradle onward, to enter some lucrative profession and to labour at it with something close to enthusiasm. The pressure is not gentle. To fail to enter such a profession is treated less as a misfortune than as an offence against respectability, as though one had appeared at church without a collar. And should a man be content with enough, preferring to stand aside, look on, and enjoy what he sees, he will find that the moment he speaks up for himself he is taken for a braggart. His modest defence of his own way of living is heard as boasting.

Yet idleness, properly understood, does not consist in doing nothing. It consists in doing a great many things that the ruling class does not happen to recognise as worthwhile. The idler is often busy enough. He is simply busy at the wrong things, wrong, that is, by the measure of those who keep the ledgers. And it seems to me that idleness has as good a right to state its case as industry has. Industry states its case daily, from every pulpit and every counting-house. Let the other side have a turn.

I understand why the turn is so rarely given. The man who will not compete for money is at once an insult and a disillusionment to those who do. He insults them by declining the prize they have spent their lives pursuing, and he disillusions them by suggesting that the prize may not be worth so much after all. A hard worker naturally resents the sight of others lounging at their ease while he toils. Alexander, the story goes, was put out by the indifference of Diogenes, who asked only that the conqueror stand out of his sunlight. The barbarians who broke into Rome found the senators sitting silent in their chairs, unmoved by the triumph of their invaders, and the barbarians were enraged by it. I sympathise with the barbarians a little. It is painful to have achieved something by enormous effort and then to find people indifferent to it.

Every pursuit has its own scorn. Physicists condemn those who know no physics. Financiers tolerate, but only on the surface, those who know little of stocks. Literary people despise the unlettered. And people of every pursuit whatever will combine, forgetting their quarrels, to disparage the man who has no pursuit at all.

Still, the resentment of the industrious is not the greatest difficulty in defending idleness. Nobody will throw you into prison for speaking against industry. You may, however, be quietly shunned for speaking foolishly, and that is a real risk. For the greatest difficulty with most subjects is simply to treat them well. Much can reasonably be said in favour of diligence; I do not deny it. But there are also arguments against diligence, and it is those I mean to set out here. To state one argument is not to ignore all the others. It is only to give one of them its hearing.

My first contention is that people should be fairly idle in their youth. A few, like Lord Macaulay, come through all the honours of school with their wits about them. But most boys pay so heavily for their academic success that they are left without resources, and they enter adult life already spent. The same cost runs through the whole period during which a young man is being educated. He is drained by the time he is finished.

When Johnson was at Oxford, an old gentleman advised him to study diligently while he was young, because reading would become irksome in old age. It was foolish advice. A great many things besides reading become irksome when we are old, and some become impossible altogether. If youth is the only time for anything, it is the time for those.

Books are good in their own way; I would not be without them. But they are a poor, bloodless substitute for life. It seems a pity to sit, like the Lady of Shalott, with one's back to the window, watching the world go by in a mirror, when one might turn round and look at it directly. And the man who reads very hard will find he has little time left over for thought.

Look back on your own schooldays. I doubt you regret a single hour you spent playing truant. What you would gladly erase are the dull, half-awake hours you passed in the classroom. The truant's hours, by contrast, can be full, vivid, and instructive.

I have sat through a great many lectures myself. I still remember learning that a spinning top is a case of kinetic stability. I remember learning that emphyteusis is not a disease, and that stillicide is not a crime. I value these scraps; I would not part with them. But I value more the things I learned in the street while I was playing truant. The street was the favourite school of Dickens and of Balzac, and it turns out every year a great many unrecognised masters in the art of understanding life. Indeed, a boy who learns nothing in the streets lacks the capacity to learn at all.

Nor need the truant go to the streets. He may wander out into the countryside instead, lie down in the grass, and fall into kindly thought, seeing the old familiar things from some new angle. That too is education, and of a genuine kind, whatever the examiners may say.
